## Practice

::: {.callout-note}

The work of this practice exercise should take a maximum of 30 minutes.

:::
#### Step 1. Why care about exploitation potential?

Reflect on the interviews - particularly where Theo talks about making technology accessible outside academia and Elin describes her team's motivation to solve the logistical problems inherent in research. 

- Did these stories match or challenge your views of what entrepreneurial exploitation is? 
- Were you aware of incubators and funding for research sector startups?

#### Step 2. Defining exploration and exploitation

Entrepreneurial process is an entire research field, but in 2017, Kuckertz et al.[^1] defined activities of exploration (sometimes called opportunity recognition) and exploitation based on a survey of academics. 

They identified six activities associated with each:

::: {.callout}
| Activity | Example | Question | 
|-----|---------| ---------|
| 1. Searching     | Regularly scanning your field or environment for opportunities | *What other startups or businesses are there in my field or area?* |
| 2. Being alert     | Having an open mind to the possibility of developing your research as an entrepreneur | *Could this finding or knowledge be applied in a startup setting?* |
| 3. Gathering information      | Getting information on startups, looking at new products and services | *How might this idea be put into practice?*
| 4. Communicating      | Talking to friends, colleagues, other entrepreneurs, innovation offices etc. about your idea | *What do you think about this idea?* |
| 5. Problem solving     | Solving a problem experienced by researchers, patients, or other population segments | *How could my research or knowledge make things easier or better for others?* |
| 6. Evaluating       | Assessing if your idea is feasible to move forward with | *Can I take the next step with my/my team's current skills, knowledge, and abilities?* |

: Exploration activities, from Kuckertz et al., 2017
:::

After testing the validity of these activities in pools of entrepreneurs and refinement of their model, the authors conclude that **Searching**, **Being alert**, and **Gathering information** are the activities that most clearly define opportunity recognition, or detecting exploitation potential.

#### Step 2. Are you detecting exploitation potential?
In a further survey, the authors linked engaging in exploration activities with being an entrepreneur. In the following self-test, evaluate how strongly you engage with detecting exploitation potential in your work.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Self-test

On a Likert scale (1 to 5, where 1 is strongly agree and 5 is strongly disagree), how much do you agree with the following questions?

1. I am always alert for opportunities to connect my research with industry.
2. I understand the potential markets that my research connects to.
3. I review my findings systematically for opportunities to connect with industry. 
4. I look for information about new ideas on products or services that are relevant in my research field.
5. I regularly scan my environment for business opportunities.
:::

Record your answers.

#### Step 3. Evaluation - The Harvard Business School Framework
In the article by Kuckertz et al., the activity of Evaluation fell between exploitation and exploration, as an activity that bridges the two processes. 

In their analytical framework for assessing entrepreneurial opportunties[^2], the Harvard Business School has 31 questions divided into a business section and a personal section to help potential entrepreneurs decide to proceed with their opportunity or not.

Read through the **personal analysis section** [(questions 21-31)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/14HGVse3kpSmSjF_MKjHQIV8f9-Ms8-4-/view?usp=sharing). Do you recognize any aspects of this decision framework in how you approach you own career, project, or other major decisions?

[^2]: Stevenson, Howard H., and Shirley Spence. "Identifying and Exploiting the Right Entrepreneurial Opportunity...For You." Harvard Business School Background Note 808-043, December 2007. (Revised June 2009.)

## Next level
#### Five (optional!) exercises for detecting exploitation potential

1. Schedule time in your calendar to prepare and submit an entry to the [2027 VentureCup contest](https://www.venturecup.se/en/), which opens in September. Bonus points for submitting together with another PULSE postdoc!

2. The [Stockholm School of Entrepreneurship (SSES)](https://www.sses.se) writes a "Research Recap" where they write about research from the entrepreneurship field. Read [this recap](https://learninglab.sses.se/research-recaps/an-activist-turn-in-entrepreneurship-education/) about refocusing entrepreneurship on activism and transforming systems.

3. Remember [Workshop 2](workshop-s2.qmd) of our 2026 annual meeting, where we played the business ethics game? Read [this paper](https://doi.org/10.1177/10422587241227072) by its creator, Gustav Hägg on making responsible choices as an entrepreneur in the exploration phase -- and how Elisabeth Holmes could have made better decisions.

4. What other startups in Sweden are there in your field? Follow two startups on your socials (BlueSky, LinkedIn, Mastodon, etc.)

5. Kuckertz et al. also identified six activities associated with exploitation - Understanding customers/markets, Planning the business, **Acquiring human resources, Setting up the organization, Developing a product/service, and Gathering resources**. Rewatch the interviews and see if you can identify the twelve activities of exploration and exploitation in Theo and Elin's stories.

[^1]: [Kuckertz et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1108/IJEBR-12-2015-0290)
